A criterion is a specific standard, rule, or factor that you use to judge, evaluate, or decide something.

Think of it this way: whenever you need to make a judgment — whether something is good or bad, whether someone qualifies for something, whether a choice is the right one — you need a measuring stick. That measuring stick is a criterion.

It answers the question: "Based on what?"

Imagine you are hiring someone for a job. You decide:

"The person must have at least 3 years of experience."

That rule — "at least 3 years of experience" — is a criterion. It is the standard you are using to judge whether a candidate qualifies.

If you also require that the person must speak two languages, that is another criterion. Now you have two criteria (more on this word in a moment) guiding your decision.
The Key Characteristics of a Criterion

To really nail the meaning, understand these three things about what makes something a criterion:

1. It is used for judgment or evaluation.
A criterion exists for the purpose of assessing something. It is not just any random fact or rule — it is specifically a rule you apply when you are evaluating, selecting, or deciding.

2. It is a specific, defined standard.
A criterion is not vague. "I want someone good" is not a criterion. "The candidate must score above 80% on the test" is a criterion, because it gives you a clear, defined line to measure against.

3. It is a single factor among possibly many.
Usually, when making a judgment, you do not rely on just one thing. You use multiple factors. Each individual factor is one criterion.
Criterion vs. Criteria — You Must Know This

This is one of the most important things to learn about this word.

Criterion is singular — it refers to one standard.
Criteria is plural — it refers to two or more standards.

❌ "The main criteria for winning is skill." (wrong — one standard, should be criterion)
✅ "The main criterion for winning is skill."

✅ "There are three criteria for passing the exam."

This is one of the most common mistakes people make in English, even educated native speakers. Many people incorrectly use "criteria" as if it were singular. Now that you know, you will always get it right.
How It Is Used in Real Life

The word "criterion" appears wherever people are making judgments, comparisons, or selections. Here are a few natural contexts:

In academics: A teacher might say, "The main criterion for grading this essay is how clearly you argue your point."

In law: A judge might apply a criterion to determine whether a law was violated — for example, whether the action was intentional.

In science: A researcher might establish a criterion for what counts as a successful experiment — for instance, a result that can be reproduced at least five times.

In everyday decisions: "My only criterion for choosing a restaurant tonight is that it must be walking distance from home."

In business: A company might have several criteria for approving a loan — credit score, income level, and employment history.
What Makes a Criterion Different from Similar Words

You might wonder how "criterion" differs from words like standard, condition, or requirement. They are related, but here is the subtle difference:

Standard is the broadest word — it refers to a general level of quality or a norm. A criterion is a specific instance of a standard applied to a judgment.

Condition often implies that something must be true for something else to happen (like a condition in a contract). A criterion is more about evaluation and comparison — it guides judgment rather than simply triggering an outcome.

Requirement means something that is mandatory — you either meet it or you don't. A criterion can be mandatory, but it can also be a factor that simply influences a decision without being a hard pass/fail rule.

In practice, these words overlap heavily, and in everyday speech, they are often used interchangeably. But technically, a criterion is most precisely a factor used in the act of judging or evaluating.
A Mental Image to Remember It

Picture a judge at a competition holding a scorecard. Each row on that scorecard — originality, technique, presentation — is a criterion. Together, all the rows are the criteria. The judge scores the competitor on every single criterion to reach a final verdict.

Whenever you see or hear the word "criterion," think: "This is one of the measuring sticks being used to make a judgment."
A criterion (plural: criteria) is a specific standard or factor that is used to judge, evaluate, or make a decision about something — it is the "based on what" behind any assessment.
